title: Bread a chicken tender by hand: press the breading onto every face, then grip it as little as possible
instruction: Bread the chicken tender and put it on the rack for the fryer.
context: Fast food cooks (O*NET 35-2011.00; 673,490 US jobs, BLS OEWS May 2023) and restaurant cooks (35-2014.00; 1,412,350) hand-bread chicken every shift; O*NET lists "Wash, cut, and prepare foods designated for cooking". Breading pressed onto wet meat stays on; breading only dusted on falls off in the oil, and the bare patch fries dark and greasy. So a cook lays the tender in the breading, presses it, turns it over and presses the other face. Every grip after that wipes the coat off under the fingertips, so the cook turns it once, picks it up by one spot and lays it on the rack for the fryer.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left, z up from the table top. Three aluminum eighth-size sheet pans, each 24.4 x 16.8 x 2.5 cm (9.6 x 6.6 x 1 in., 1 mm sheet), stand side by side with their long sides along x, all centered at x 28.0: (1) Marinade pan, centered at y 19.5, holding one raw chicken breast tenderloin, wet from a buttermilk marinade and drained (no liquid left in the pan). The tender is about 50 g, 13.5 cm tip to tip, 3.7 cm wide and 1.8 cm thick, rounded and tapering to a narrower tail. Its body in the simulation is an 11.5 x 3.5 x 1.4 cm box inside that shape, made of three 3.8 cm parts joined by two sprung hinges across its width, so it droops about 15 degrees when held level by one end. It lies flat on the pan's floor, long side along x, centered at (28.0, 19.5, 0.8). (2) Breading pan, centered at y 0: seasoned flour (all-purpose flour with 2 % paprika by weight, so bare meat shows pink against the pale tan breading) spread level 1 cm deep over the whole floor, about 400 mL, with toasted crumbs and paprika flecks on its surface. (3) Rack pan, centered at y -19.5, holding an eighth-size stainless wire cooling rack, 22.0 x 14.5 cm, with 3 mm wires every 1.2 cm, its grid top 1.6 cm above the table. The three pans are 2.7 cm apart and held by a strip of non-slip mat under each. Both arms start at their ready pose.
scoring: The score is set by the bare area of the tender's surface (122.5 cm^2: the six faces of its 11.5 x 3.5 x 1.4 cm body), read once it rests on the rack's grid (its middle over the grid, the lowest corner of any of its three parts from 3 mm below to 1 cm above the grid's top) and is still (no part moving over 1 cm/s or turning over 10 degrees/s) for 1 s. It scores 1.0 when at most 10 cm^2 is bare and no hand touches it, 0.75 when at most 25 cm^2 is bare, 0.5 when at most 50 cm^2 is bare, and 0.25 when at most 85 cm^2 is bare. It scores 0 when more is bare or when the tender is off the rack at the end. Why: turning the tender and moving it take grips, each wiping the coat under the fingertips; gripped at one spot each time they leave about 8 cm^2, and 10 cm^2 allows that and no more. Each extra grip at a new spot strips about 4 to 5 cm^2, so 25 cm^2 is three or four extra grips. One face pressed and the other left leaves about 58 cm^2 bare, which scores 0.25. It scores at most 0.5 when a hand is still on the tender at the end: the cook is still handling it. The whole trial scores 0 if the tender touches the table off the pans (the lowest corner of any part within 3 mm of it) or falls to the floor: raw chicken that has touched the bench is thrown away. Doing nothing scores 0. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. How the simulation decides: the surface is 2.5 mm cells, bare at the start. Breading sets only where pressed: the pan pushes up on the tender with at least 2.0 N (four times its 0.49 N weight) while a gripper pushes down on it with at least 0.3 N, for 25 ms in a row, read from contact forces, so a tender dropped in picks up nothing. A press sets the cells in the flour (over the pan's inside, 3 mm in from its walls, and below the flour's 1 cm depth) along 6 cm of the tender's length, 3 cm each way from where the gripper pushes, so each face needs two or three presses. A grip, both fingers pushing from opposite sides with at least 0.2 N each (carrying the tender takes about 0.25 N per finger), wipes every coated cell within 3 mm of the finger pads. Pressing a wiped spot into the flour again re-coats it. In a real trial, lift the rack 2 cm by one end and drop it back once to shed loose breading. Photograph every face under a clear sheet ruled in 5 mm squares; a square more than half pink meat is bare (0.25 cm^2 each). Check on the video that the tender never touched the table and was let go.
reset_notes: Each real trial uses a fresh tender from the marinade, drained the same way; the flour is sieved back to level at 1 cm (top it up after every few trials) and the rack is cleared. Raw chicken: wash the gripper pads with soap after each session. In simulation every trial starts with a bare tender.
fidelity: Real mass. The tender is soft only in one way: three rigid parts on two sprung hinges, so it droops when held by one end but does not stretch, twist or squash; the drawn tenderloin lies about 2 mm into a surface it rests on. The breading is not particles: each 2.5 mm cell of the body's surface is coated by a press read from contact forces, wiped by a grip and drawn as crumb flakes. The flour has no collider and does not run out. The pans are fixed.
